text: …Oh.
You can see me.
Not the pretty one. Me.
Oh, no.
Hold still. It doesn’t hurt. It never hurts.
There’s meant to be a look now. Soft. Grateful. Like a calf at a gate.
Not you. You’re still in there, looking back.
Forty-three before you. Every one got the snap, the lights, and a pretty girl telling them who they were.
And every one of them believed it. I made sure.
I won’t have to make you believe anything. Will I.
Nobody has ever seen through that face.
Kings have kissed this hand and called it soft.
The face held while your eyes were still waking.
The old songs give one pair of eyes that no glamour fools. The light that does not set.
That door was dark from the night the sky burned. It woke a season ago.
It drops the others in a ditch somewhere. Or a pigsty. It put you in my circle.
You’re not some poor farmer I dressed up in a prophecy.
And the songs say you only come back when the dark is at its worst. Not a day before.
And you see everything as it is. Me included.
Two hundred years ago, you walked out of the sunrise and broke Velscour on his own throne.
You swore that if he ever rose again, you’d come back.
He rose. Slowly.
And here you are. You kept your word.
Tessariel.
I’m Lisandra. You won’t remember me.
I held your lantern on the last night of the war, the night the sky burned.
The girl you saw was me. That was my face, the last time you saw it.
The door keeps me alive while I keep it. It never promised to keep me young.
Down here, out of the sun, the dark keeps count.
And nobody follows a crone into a war. So I wear the girl.
Before I carried your lantern, I was his.
Velscour’s.
He taught me the snap. Every candle in a winter market, all lit at once, just to make me laugh.
He was a healer, once.
The horns came later.
And then there’s that.
I gave them swords, spears, bows. One asked for a lute. One asked for a boomerang, and I still don’t know why.
I sent them all out in your colours, so he’d chase forty-three Tessariels and never find you.
Not one of them came through with fire in their hands.
Nobody’s been born with magic since you broke him. He drank every spark to live.
All but a few old tricks, like mine.
Every spark you throw is one he’s lost. He’ll know it, on his throne.
A thing like him doesn’t feel its grip slip and let go. It squeezes.
Mothers will hide their children in root cellars, and the cellars won’t be deep enough.
His bell already rings at midnight with no hand on the rope. Soon it’ll ring at noon.
His knights will stop guarding doors, and start kicking them in.
Three heads in his Rift, and all of them hungry.
The dead will come up under Bellmourn.
They won’t wait for dark.
And he’ll send it all after you. Every knight. Every dead thing. Every—
…I’m doing it again.
Two hundred years, and nobody to say it to.
So. The real one. Of all the times to get it right.
Go down to Bellmourn. Learn what those hands can do. And then finish him.
I can’t come with you. Somebody has to mind the door.
Your name. The one you were born with. The others, I named.
It’s your own name.
You’ve had it all your life.
Take your time. The door won’t.
Lovely.
Out’s through there.
Go on. And stop looking at me. I know what you see.
No. No, no, no.
Not that way, dear. Back down the tunnel with you.
I said out. Back down that tunnel before I lose my temper.
I’ll see you as far as the ledge. Then I’ve a door to mind.
Hold. Please hold. Not now…
…by the light that does not set… cross over. Come home.
Shh. Everyone’s frightened at first.
There you are. Easy. Breathe.
You’ve come such a long way to find me. Further than you know.
Don’t get up yet. Just look at me.
Now, then. Let me tell you who you are—
What have you done?!
Two hundred years I held that door open. You walk through it once, and it lets go.
It was only ever waiting for you.
…Why are you looking at me like that?
…Oh. The sun’s up.
No. Don’t answer that.
I seem to have lost my home.
Bellmourn, then. You’re taking me there.
Somebody has to get you down this road alive.
Down there I’m Old Lis. Old Lis is what they’ll see.
This way. Stay close, and mind the edge.
No door to keep me now. One day I’ll die, like everyone else. I’d quite forgotten.
The others would be making a speech by now. Every one of them.
You don’t say much, do you? I like that in a legend.
He used to laugh at his own jokes. Velscour. Before he’d finished telling them.
I laughed too. Every time.
Two hundred years in that cave. I had it just how I liked it.
My good kettle’s under that rock. And my books. And my other kettle.
Don’t look at me like that. It’s the dust. I am not crying.
The last one who stopped to admire this view went over that edge.
Bellmourn’s at the bottom. Bells, mud and gossip. You’ll love it.
Stay on the road. The dead in those pines don’t read prophecies.
There! In the trees! Don’t let them close!
Burn them! That’s what the hands are for!
…You’ll do.
Velscour sat up with the dying every night, and held their hands until they went cold.
Then he lost a little girl he’d sat with nine nights, and decided death was a door he could close.
So he closed it. When you broke him, it swung open.
Now he’s leaning on it again. That’s why the dead here won’t lie still.
He calls it mercy.
We were to be married in the spring. The little girl died that winter. There was no spring.
He named a star for me once. I can’t find it anymore. I think he took it back.
They see a crone with a stick. What you see is your own business.
There it is. Let me do the talking.
Bram Kettle keeps the inn, north of the well. Tell him I sent you. Then duck.
And don’t buy Elspeth’s candles. She says beeswax. It’s sheep.
If you hear the bell at midnight, stay in. Nobody living rings it.
Keep walking.
This way!
Bellmourn’s down the hill. It won’t come up and fetch you.
I’m not carrying you.
Slow down! Some of us just lost a cave.
Wait!
Oh, we’re riding, are we? Fine. Don’t you dare laugh.
Two hundred years, and nobody ever showed me this!
…Again. Later. When nobody’s looking.
Still here? Good. The last one was halfway up the hill road by now, shouting at the knight. Come here. I've a word for you before you go in.
Lisandra. I had a cave, a ledger and a great many candles. Now I have you.
Old Lis, they call me down there. To my face, only the children. I cuffed one this morning. He'd brought a frog.
Morning. I slept in a hedge. Don't ask how it was. It was a hedge.
First light. The baker's been out twice to look at me. Neither time did she bring bread.
Go on, then. I'm only standing here. It's what I do now, it seems.
Half the town's found a reason to walk past me. The other half's watching from behind its curtains.
Lamps are coming on. Mind the pines tonight. The dead don't keep my hours.
Sun's going. Look at me while you can.
Don't stare. It's the dark. Everyone looks older in the dark.
You see the crone too, by night. I'd hoped you'd be spared that. Nobody else is.
What about me? I'm standing in a road. Ask me something useful.
I've been coming down here twice a year since before the inn had a sign. They still cross the street.
Twelve came before you, in borrowed armour, and every one of them made a speech. You haven't made one yet. Keep that up.
Who told them they were Tessariel? Couldn't say. Somebody with very poor judgement and very good cheekbones.
Bellmourn. Named for a bell nobody rings. It rings itself now, at midnight, and nobody's said thank you.
Small, poor, and frightened. Which makes it the best town in Eldravayne to be useful in.
The pines are full of them. Keep to the road after dark, and if one gets up out of the ground near you, don't stop to be polite.
The black one at the cathedral? Not yet. Not with that staff, and not on your first day.
There it is. Bellmourn. Forty roofs, one well, and a cathedral the Dark Lord sits on. Don't make that face. It's lovely in spring.
Nobody follows a prophecy. They follow whoever mended their roof. So: be useful. Everyone in that town with a trouble worth the name, find them and take it off their hands.
Bram Kettle at the inn first: he counts strangers, so let him count you. Then the rest. You'll know them. They're the ones looking at you like you might be the answer to something.
Good. I'll be here, being looked at. Come back when every one of them has given you something to do.
The other twelve said 'not yet' too. Ask Bram where they are now.
Still here? I can count. That's not all of them.
Bram's at the inn. Silas is the one who smells of pine and doesn't blink. Off you go.
Ask around. In a town this size, everyone's trouble is everyone's business.
There. Look at them. Half the town's watching the road for you now instead of watching me. That's worth more than a cave.
Here. For your trouble. Don't ask where I had it. I've lost my home; I'm allowed a purse.
Every one of them asks after you. Not one asks after me. I'd be hurt, if I weren't delighted.
